Large language models builds on top of autoregressive transformers to predict the next token.
This is often because these models are trained to “hillclimb” this specific objective, and with the recent advancement in RL we’ve basically achieved pseudo-intellectualism
There are also a whole genre of language model built on top of diffusion blocks, where it learns to reconstruct masked tokens, then generates text through repeated unmaskingdiffusion is an alternate approach to AR, but if anything it lacks the coherency formed via superposition to those of AR models (i suspect) (Nie et al., 2025).
Speculative decoding techniques such as DFlash uses a lightweight block-diffusion draft model to produce a block of draft tokens in one forward pass for an autoregressive target model to verify (Chen et al., 2026).

Most variants of LLMs are decoder-only (Radford et al., 2019). There are bi-directional encoder-decoder models, though their application are more domain-specific, whereas decoder-only models generalized a lot better, per recent history.

Optimization

Quantization: reduce computational and memory costs of running inference with representing the weight and activations with low-precision data type
Continuous batching: update the batch after each decoding step so finished requests leave and waiting requests can join. Orca introduced iteration-level scheduling. PagedAttention manages KV-cache memory in blocks; it can support this scheduling by reducing wasted memory.
Different Attention variants, for better kernels and hardware optimisation (Think of Flash Attention 3, Radix Attention, TreeAttention, etc.)
Byte-Latent Transformer: group bytes into variable-length patches using next-byte prediction entropy. The large transformer processes patches, while a smaller decoder generates bytes autoregressively. 1

A small byte-level model estimates how uncertain the next byte is. High uncertainty starts a new patch; predictable byte sequences can share longer patches, reducing the number of steps run by the large transformer. Entropy determines patch boundaries. Byte generation still uses the decoder’s next-byte predictions. See 2412.09871⁠ (Pagnoni et al., 2024) . ↩
